{{Short description|Theorem concerning occurrences of terminal symbols in context-free languages}}
In [[theoretical computer science]], '''Parikh's theorem''' states that if one looks only at the number of occurrences of each [[Context-free grammar#Formal definitions|terminal symbol]] in a [[context-free language]], without regard to their order, then the language is indistinguishable from a [[regular language]].<ref name="kozen">{{cite book |title=Automata and Computability|last=Kozen |first=Dexter|year=1997 |publisher=Springer-Verlag|location=New York|isbn=3-540-78105-6}}</ref> It is useful for deciding that strings with a given number of terminals are not accepted by a context-free grammar.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www8.cs.umu.se/kurser/TDBC92/VT06/final/3.pdf|title=Parikh's theorem|author=Håkan Lindqvist|publisher=Umeå Universitet}}</ref> It was first proved by [[Rohit Jivanlal Parikh|Rohit Parikh]] in 1961<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Parikh |first1=Rohit|authorlink=Rohit Jivanlal Parikh|year=1961 |title=Language Generating Devices|journal=Quarterly Progress Report, Research Laboratory of Electronics, MIT}}</ref> and republished in 1966.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Parikh |first1=Rohit|authorlink=Rohit Jivanlal Parikh|year=1966 |title=On Context-Free Languages|journal=Journal of the [[Association for Computing Machinery]]|volume=13|issue=4|pages=570–581|doi=10.1145/321356.321364|s2cid=12263468|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Definitions and formal statement==
Let <math>\Sigma=\{a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_k\}</math> be an [[Alphabet (formal languages)|alphabet]]. The ''Parikh vector'' of a word <math>w</math> is defined as its image under the function <math display=inline>p:\Sigma^*\to\mathbb{N}^k</math>, given by<ref name="kozen"/> 
<math display=block>p(w)=(|w|_{a_1}, |w|_{a_2}, \ldots, |w|_{a_k})</math>
where <math>|w|_{a_i}</math> denotes the number of occurrences of the symbol <math>a_i</math> in the word <math>w</math>.

A subset of <math>\mathbb{N}^k</math> is said to be ''linear'' if it is of the form
<math display=block>u_0 + \mathbb{N}u_1 + \dots + \mathbb{N}u_m = \{u_0+t_1u_1+\dots+t_mu_m \mid t_1,\ldots,t_m\in\mathbb{N}\}</math>
for some vectors <math display=inline>u_0,\ldots,u_m</math>.
A subset of <math>\mathbb{N}^k</math> is said to be ''semi-linear'' if it is a union of finitely many linear subsets.

{{Math theorem|name=Theorem|note=|math_statement=
Let <math>L</math> be a context-free language or a regular language, let <math>P(L)</math> be the set of Parikh vectors of words in <math>L</math>, that is, <math display=inline>P(L) = \{p(w) \mid w \in L\}</math>.  Then <math>P(L)</math> is a semi-linear set.

If <math>S</math> is any semi-linear set, then there exists a regular language (which a fortiori is context-free) whose Parikh vectors is <math>S</math>. 
}}
In short, the image under <math>p</math> of context-free languages and of regular languages is the same, and it is equal to the set of [[semilinear set]]s.

Two languages are said to be ''commutatively equivalent'' if they have the same set of Parikh vectors. Thus, every context-free language is commutatively equivalent to some regular language.

== Proof ==

The second part is easy to prove.
{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof=
Given semi-linear set <math>S</math>, to construct a regular language whose set of Parikh vectors is <math>S</math>.

<math>S</math> is a union of 0 or more linear sets. Since the empty language is regular, and union of regular languages is regular, it suffices to prove that any linear set is the set of Parikh vectors of a regular language.

Let <math>S = \{u_0+t_1u_1+\dots+t_mu_m \mid t_1,\ldots,t_m\in\mathbb{N}\}</math>, then it is the set of Parikh vectors of <math>\{z_0\} \cdot (\cup_{i=1}^m \{z_i\})^*</math>, where each <math>z_i</math> has Parikh vector <math>u_i</math>.
}}

The first part is less easy. The following proof is credited to Goldstine.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Goldstine |first=J. |date=1977-01-01 |title=A simplified proof of parikh's theorem |url=https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/0012-365X%2877%2990103-0 |journal=Discrete Mathematics |language=en |volume=19 |issue=3 |pages=235–239 |doi=10.1016/0012-365X(77)90103-0 |issn=0012-365X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> 

First we need a small strengthening of the [[pumping lemma for context-free languages]]:

{{Math theorem
| name = Lemma
| note = 
| math_statement = If <math>L</math> is generated by a Chomsky normal form grammar, then <math>\exists N \geq 1</math>, such that the following is true.

For any <math>k \geq 1</math>, and for any <math>w \in L</math> with <math>|w| \geq N^k</math>, given a derivation <math>S \Rightarrow^* uAv</math> of <math>w</math> from the axiom <math>S</math>, we can split <math>w</math> into segments <math>w = ux_1\cdots x_kzy_k\cdots y_1v</math>, and pick a nonterminal symbol <math>A</math>, such that we have: 

<math display="block">|x_iy_i|\geq 1</math> for all <math>i</math>, and <math>|x_1\cdots x_kzy_k\cdots y_1| \leq N^k</math>

and the derivation <math>S \Rightarrow^* uAv</math> can be split in the following (with the same parse tree, in particular using precisely the same nonterminals):

<math display="block">S \Rightarrow^* uAv\quad  \forall i, A \Rightarrow^* x_iAy_i A \Rightarrow^* z\quad </math>
}}

The proof is essentially the same as the standard pumping lemma: use the pigeonhole principle to find <math>k</math> copies of some nonterminal symbol <math>A</math> in the longest path in the shortest derivation tree.

Now we prove the first part of Parikh's theorem, making use of the above lemma.

{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof=

First, construct a Chomsky normal form grammar for <math>L</math>.

For each finite nonempty subset of nonterminals <math>U</math>, define <math>L_U</math> to be the set of sentences in <math>L</math> such that there exists a derivation that uses every nonterminal in <math>U</math>, no more and no less. It is clear that <math>L = \cup_U L_U</math>, so it suffices to prove that each <math>p(L_U)</math> is a semilinear set.  

Now fix some <math>U</math>, and let <math>k = |U|</math>. We construct two finite sets <math>F, G</math>, such that <math>p(L_U) = p(F\cdot G^*)</math>, which is obviously semilinear.  

: For notational clarity, write <math>\Rightarrow^*_U</math> to mean "there exists a derivation using no more (but possibly less) than nonterminals in <math>U</math>. With that, we define <math>F, G</math> as follows:  
<math display="block">F = \{w \in L_U: |w| < N^k\}</math>
<math display="block">G = \{xy: 1 \leq |xy| \leq N^k \text{ and there exists } A\in U \text{ such that } A \Rightarrow^*_U xAy\}</math>

To prove <math>p(L_U) \subset p(F\cdot G^*)</math>, we induct on the length of <math>w\in L_U</math>.

: If <math>|w| < N^k</math>, then <math>w \in F</math>, so <math>p(w) \in p(F\cdot G^*)</math>. Otherwise, since <math>w \in L_U</math>, there is a derivation of <math>w</math> using precisely the elements of <math>U</math>. By the strengthened pumping lemma, this derivation can be rewritten to be of the form  

<math display="block">S 
		  \underset{d_0}{\stackrel{*}{\Rightarrow}}  u A v 
		  \underset{d_1}{\stackrel{*}{\Rightarrow}}  u x_1 A y_1 v 
		  \underset{d_2}{\stackrel{*}{\Rightarrow}} \cdots 
		  \underset{d_{k}}{\stackrel{*}{\Rightarrow}} u x_1 \cdots x_k A y_k \cdots y_1 v 
		  \underset{d_{k+1}}{\stackrel{*}{\Rightarrow}}  u x_1 \cdots x_k z y_k \cdots y_1 v</math>
: where <math>A\in U</math>, <math>1 \leq |x_iy_i|</math>, and <math>|x_1 \cdots x_k z y_k \cdots y_1| \leq N^k</math>.  

: Since there are only <math>k-1</math> elements in <math>U\setminus \{A\}</math>, but there are <math>k</math> sub-derivations <math>d_1, ..., d_k</math> in the middle, picking one witnessing subderivation to use each of the nonterminals in <math>U\setminus \{A\}</math>, we may delete one sub-derivation <math>d_i</math> and obtain a shorter <math>w'</math> that still uses all the nonterminals of <math>U</math>, i.e., which is still in <math>L_U</math>, with   

<math display="block">p(w) = p(uzv) + p(x_1y_1) + \cdots + p(x_ky_k) = p(w') + p(x_iy_i)</math>

: By induction, <math>p(w')  \in p(F\cdot G^*)</math>, and by construction, <math>x_iy_i\in G</math>, so <math>p(w)\in p(F\cdot G^*)</math>.  

To prove <math>p(L_U) \supset p(F\cdot G^*)</math>, consider an element <math>w\in F\cdot G^*</math>. We need to show that <math>p(w) \in p(L_U)</math>. We induct on the minimal number of factors from <math>G</math> that is needed to identify <math>w</math> as an element of <math>F\cdot G^*</math>.  

: If no factor from <math>G</math> is needed, then <math>w \in F \subset L_U</math>.  

: Otherwise, <math>w = w'xy</math> for some <math>w'\in F\cdot G^*</math> and <math>xy\in G</math>, where <math>w'</math> requires less factors from <math>G</math> than <math>w</math>.  

: By induction, <math>p(w') = p(w'')</math> for some <math>w''\in L_U</math>. By construction of <math>G</math>, there exists some <math>A\in U</math> such that <math>A\Rightarrow^*_U xAy</math>.  

: By construction of <math>L_U</math>, the symbol <math>A</math> appears in a derivation of <math>w''</math> using exactly all of <math>U</math>. Then we can interpolate <math>A\Rightarrow^*_U xAy</math> into that derivation to obtain some <math>w'''\in L_U</math> such that  

<math display="block">p(w''') = p(w'') + p(xy) = p(w') + p(xy) = p(w)</math>

}}

==Strengthening for bounded languages==
A language <math>L</math> is ''bounded'' if <math>L\subset w_1^*\ldots w_k^*</math> for some fixed words <math>w_1,\ldots, w_k</math>.
Ginsburg and Spanier <ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ginsburg|first1=Seymour|last2=Spanier|first2=Edwin H.|year=1966 |title=Presburger formulas, and languages|journal=Pacific Journal of Mathematics|volume=16|issue=2|pages=285–296|doi=10.2140/pjm.1966.16.285|url=https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.pjm/1102994974|doi-access=free}}</ref>
gave a necessary and sufficient condition, similar to Parikh's theorem, for bounded languages.

Call a linear set ''stratified'', if in its definition for each <math>i\ge 1</math> the vector <math>u_i</math> has the property that it has at most two non-zero coordinates, and for each <math>i,j\ge 1</math> if each of the vectors <math>u_i,u_j</math> has two non-zero coordinates, <math>i_1<i_2</math> and <math>j_1<j_2</math>, respectively, then their order is ''not'' <math>i_1<j_1<i_2<j_2</math>.
A semi-linear set is stratified if it is a union of finitely many stratified linear subsets.

{{Math theorem|name=Ginsburg-Spanier|note=|math_statement= 
A bounded language <math>L</math> is context-free if and only if <math>\{(n_1,\ldots,n_k)\mid w_1^{n_1}\ldots w_k^{n_k}\in L\}</math> is a stratified semi-linear set.
}}

==Significance==
The theorem has multiple interpretations. It shows that a context-free language over a singleton alphabet must be a [[regular language]] and that some context-free languages can only have [[ambiguous grammar]]s{{explain|reason=why exactly?|date=April 2017}}. Such languages are called ''[[inherently ambiguous language]]s''. From a [[formal grammar]] perspective, this means that some ambiguous [[context-free grammar]]s cannot be converted to equivalent unambiguous context-free grammars.
